basicamente joga isso no seu claude e ele entende (opus 5.5 max effort):

Edit my talking-head video into a polished YouTube video with explanatory motion graphics.  INPUT - Raw video: <path/to/raw.mp4>. Speech is Portuguese; don't translate. - Target: at most <6:30>. Style: premium, clean, editorial ("Anthropic/Apple level"). - End card: subscribe + follow me on X (<https://t.co/tSjKsZveHR>) + "comment what you want to see next". - Never cover my face. Never show where I live.  STACK - Remotion (https://t.co/RONMuXavg6) for the composition, ffmpeg for cuts and encoding, Python for analysis. - Transcribe with word timestamps using ElevenLabs Scribe. It has precise word boundaries and marks fillers like "hã"/"é". - If you use Whisper instead: its word ends stretch over pauses, so refine every cut point with the audio energy.  1) PLAN THE CUT - Make an indexed transcript (word index → text, start, end). - Choose keep-ranges by word index. Remove fillers, false starts, repeated sentences and weak tangents until it fits the target. - Put the strongest line (2–4 s) at the very start as a cold-open hook.  2) CUT, FRAME-ACCURATE AND IN SYNC - Cut points:   - Cut in the silence between words, never inside a word.   - Keep ~50 ms before the first word and ~60 ms after the last word (~160 ms if it ends a sentence). - Silences inside kept ranges:   - Detect them with a 10 ms RMS envelope. A threshold around −38 dBFS worked here; measure your own noise floor first.   - Shorten any pause over 0.32 s to 0.22 s (0.36 s after a sentence ends). - Round every boundary to whole frames (30 fps) and merge touching segments. - Video: ffmpeg split → trim(start_frame, end_frame) → concat, plus a light grade (hqdn3d, eq, colorbalance, unsharp) → intermediate at CRF 14. - Audio: cut the same boundaries in numpy with 8 ms fades and no overlap. A/V stays in sync. - QA: re-transcribe the cut and diff it against the intended text. Fix leaked fragments and clipped word starts, then repeat until clean.  3) FACE TRACK - Detect the face every 0.2 s (Apple Vision or MediaPipe). - Smooth with a moving average inside each cut segment, never across a jump cut. - Use it to frame the camera and to place graphics on the side away from the face.  4) DESIGN SYSTEM - One palette: dark warm stage #14120F, ivory "paper" #F1ECE2, one accent (clay #D97A4E). - Fonts: Fraunces (serif display), Inter Tight (UI), JetBrains Mono (labels). Add subtle grain and soft glows. - No gradient text, no neon. - Camera layout modes, morphing between them in ~0.7 s (cubic in-out):   - full frame;   - split left/right: rounded camera card 856×936, face at 42% of its height, graphics on the other half;   - PIP: 256 px circle over a full-screen paper sheet, for chapter moments.  5) BEAT SHEET (JSON) - Give every sentence group a visual, cued to word start times in the cut timeline:   - lower third (name/role);   - big numbers with count-up;   - lists that reveal on each spoken item;   - SVG diagrams that draw on;   - timeline, before→after, comparison cards, quotes;   - arrows annotating objects in the room. - Structure: cold open with kinetic captions → 1.5 s title card → content → end card (CTAs plus a portrait still).  6) BUILD IN REMOTION - One composition, 1920×1080 at 30 fps. Put `<OffthreadVideo>` (muted) inside a container whose rect and transform come from the layout keyframes plus the face track. - Each graphic is a `<Sequence>` component. Drive reveals with useCurrentFrame + interpolate/spring (opacity, translateY, blur). - SVG draw-on: animate strokeDashoffset using the real path length. - Jump cuts: alternate zoom 1.0 ↔ 1.075 around the face when the picture jumps. Add a 1–2% slow breathing zoom elsewhere and a punch-in on punchlines. - Deterministic only: no Math.random. - Check key frames with `npx remotion still`: face uncovered, no clipped text, nothing appearing before its cue.  7) SOUND - Voice: highpass 80 Hz, light denoise, −2.5 dB at 280 Hz, +2 dB at 3.6 kHz, de-ess, 3:1 compressor. - Music: royalty-free lo-fi (e.g. Mixkit). Change track per section with 4 s crossfades.   - Duck 9–12 dB under the voice in the speech band, keeping the lows.   - Louder only on the title and end cards. - SFX: very subtle whooshes on layout changes, pops on reveals, ticks on counters. - Master: two-pass loudnorm to −14 LUFS, true peak −1.5.  8) RENDER, VERIFY, DELIVER - Encode: H.264 CRF 16, AAC 320k, BT.709, +faststart. - Verify:   - duration within the target, −14 LUFS;   - no frozen stretch over 0.3 s;   - a 40-frame contact sheet;   - re-transcribe the final mix: at least 95% of words should match, so the music isn't masking the voice. - Deliver the MP4, an .srt from the word timings (max 42 chars per line, 2 lines), and YouTube chapters (first at 0:00, each at least 10 s).  RULES - Show numbers and claims exactly as I say them. - Check names and spellings on the web before they go on screen. - No invented stats or testimonials. - Short, concrete on-screen copy with no AI clichés. - Don't publish anything without my OK.

Claude Code can now make full videos from your terminal..

Not slideshows. Not text on screen..

Actual motion graphics with animations, transitions, custom photos, and background music.

[ SHARED A TUTORIAL BELOW EDITED WITH THIS SETUP IN JUST 5mins ]

▫️Here's the setup: 

Claude Code + Remotion

Remotion is a React based framework that renders video programmatically.

You describe what you want in plain English, Claude writes the React components and Remotion renders it into a real MP4.

What you can actually do with this:

> Generate 9:16 vertical videos for TikTok / Reels / Shorts 
> Add animated text with viral hooks and safe zones 
> Pull live web screenshots directly into your scenes using Chrome MCP 
> Fact-check your content in real time with Perplexity MCP 
> Drop in your own photos and background music 
> Edit existing talking-head footage cut bloopers, add captions 
> Schedule posts to your socials straight from the terminal

▫️How to set it up (takes 5 minutes) :

> Make sure you have Node.js installed ( node -v  to check )
> Create a new Remotion project: 
npx create-video@latest
Pick the Blank template, enable TailwindCSS, and install the Skills package when prompted.
> Install dependencies:
cd my-video
npm install
> Start the preview server: npm run dev
> Open Claude Code in the same project folder:
cd my-video
claude

That's it. You can now prompt videos in plain English.

If you already have a Remotion project, just add the skill directly:

npx skills add remotion-dev/skills

This drops a SKILL.md into your project that gives Claude expert knowledge of Remotion.. animations, compositions, captions, assets, 3D content everything.

Example prompt you can steal:

"Create a 30-second 9:16 vertical video about the top 3 AI tools this week. Use animated text with a hook in the first 2 seconds. Add smooth transitions between scenes. Keep text in the safe zone for TikTok. Use a dark tech aesthetic with blue accent colors."

Claude writes all the React code, renders a preview, you tweak with natural language, and export when ready.

The crazy part is this whole pipeline is local, free (minus your Claude sub), and you never open a video editor.

This guy has been EVERYWHERE on my timeline recently, and as someone who's been editing for over a decade and full-time since the pandemic, imo he's massively overselling what AI can do.

Cutting bad takes and silences with software isn't a revolutionary new thing. I use a program called Gling, which auto-transcribes my video, removes dead air, and then attempts to detect and cut all the bad takes automatically. The attempt is never perfect, but it's pretty solid, and having my recording laid out as text I can interact with makes corrections way faster than if I had to listen back through the recording. I then take it into Premiere Pro, and use a script I wrote myself to trim out any leftover silent frames so that the edit is as tight as possible.

Here's the thing: I've been doing this for years. And Gling is still better at it than what he's showing off here.

And ngl, it's awesome to be able to automate this part away, there's nothing creative or fun about scrubbing through your bad takes and chopping them out by hand. The same applies to things like importing and syncing up all your clips and audio, refining subtitles, etc. I wrote a bunch of scripts to help with stuff like this, I'm not surprised that AI can do it as well, and as far as I'm concerned, this is great. It's doing what computers are supposed to be doing: handling the tedious busywork.

When I make a Pokémon video, I don't import hundreds of Pokémon images and stick their Type-matched backgrounds behind them in the timeline by hand every time. I click on their Google Images result, and press the "import Pokémon" button I coded for myself. If ChatGPT or Claude can give someone who doesn't know how to script that same ability, cool, I have a hard time getting upset at that.

This is also, like, 10% of the process of making many types of video. The rest of it, the part that isn't just busywork, is something AI is still mediocre-to-terrible at unless you're making unbelievably basic stuff, the stuff that you were already at risk of being ousted from because anyone with basic experience could replace you.

That unbelievably basic stuff is, unfortunately, going to start getting handed over to AI instead of external editors. I'm not saying it's a good thing, in fact it really sucks, but I also live in reality. As soon as the person who recorded the footage realizes they can give their video file to Astra and pop out a whatever video, they're not going to hand it over to a human editor to do the same thing. Again: I'd much rather these low grade edits continue to create work for people, but humans follow the path of least resistance so it is absolutely, 100% coming.

The good news is, you can safeguard against this simply by NOT handing back whatever videos. There still are, and will continue to be, plenty of people out there who care about making the videos GOOD, and distinctive, and have an actual voice. This is something AI is totally, 100% incapable of right now, and likely will be for as long as it's based on neural networks; by their very nature they will always default down to middle-of-the-road swill. This dude's doing, as far as I can tell, content that's largely talking head and basic B-roll that doesn't particularly need elements like funny jokes or interesting visuals, but he's taken that and extrapolated it to a statement as sweeping as "I'm not sure I'd bother teaching a kid to edit anymore," which, in my opinion, is completely unreasonable.

If you're an editor, the better you are at the fundamentally human elements, the better off you'll be. And really, this is how it's always worked to some extent. You do need to start stepping your game up though, now. You need to be better at editing than AI is, but fortunately this really isn't a tall order.

I'll also note: EVEN THE BUSYWORK is still only partway there. I've gone through some of this guy's other AI editing content, as well as looked at other sources, and... man, I'm not impressed. "Hey computer, on your last pass you chopped off half the first word of this sentence, next time make sure you go in and correct it." Or, hear me out dude: how about you just go into the timeline and fix it yourself??? It literally takes less time than saying that sentence. This kind of stuff will become less of an issue as models get more refined, but we're sure as hell not there yet.

Also, on a personal note, I will say that I know this guy has a pedigree behind him, but I'm inherently set up to distrust someone who has stuff like "obsessed with making perfect videos" in his bio. It reeks of hustle bro culture, and then when I see his AI-edited stuff coming out thoroughly unimpressive, with bland visuals that would be a rough cut starting point on my relatively smaller channels, it casts doubt on that statement.

And then you go to the comments about these videos that he "handed off to AI and walked away from." And what do you see? He's telling one person that actually, he still had to do a ton of his own work. And then he's telling another person that actually, for the style of video they create, this workflow probably wouldn't work at all. And now I find myself wondering what the hell point he was ever trying to make.

text:
how to get your app a viral tiktok, from 69,674 videos we posted last year:

209 of them (0.3%) drove 64.6% of our 755M views. virality is a numbers game you can rig. here's how we find the winners fast and squeeze them dry:

before you post

1. one brand new account per creator per app.

2. days 1-3, don't post. scroll the niche 1-2 hours, watch 10+ videos to the end, like 20-30, leave 3-5 real comments, follow 5-10 accounts.

3. days 3-4, post one broad video ("realizing how much money i spent last month"). then 1 campaign video a day, aiming for 200+ views in the first 24 hours.

4. 9 out of 10 "shadowbans" aren't real. it's a cold account, a flagged keyword, a duplicate edit or a bad hook. you can reuse footage but  can't reuse the cut.

research

5. find your star feature, the 1-2 things the app is built around. your real competitor is whoever markets that feature. ex: parrot's is swiping, so tiktok is on its list.

6. save viral videos in 3 buckets: your niche, your star-feature competitors, viral ugc in general. only organically viral ones, no ad spend behind them.

7. 9 times out of 10 you can tweak a viral general ugc format to fit your app.

formats

8. run all 4: wall of text, talking head, slideshow, hook + demo.

9. talking heads take longer to pop, then convert more because the viewer trusts the person. they get flagged as ads way less too.

10. slideshows are the easiest product placement. people swipe to the end, so the app slide almost always gets seen.

11. hook + demo: take your best wall of text, cut it to a 3-second hook, show the app at the end.

12. read the comments on your wall of text videos. they double as a free focus group.

hooks

13. open on a problem your audience has lived, felt in that exact spot.

14. the best ones split the room. jenni ai pulled a 3.6M-view video by pulling in people who use ai for essays and people who judge them for it.

15. skip shock bait. the comments fill up with the bait and the video gets pushed to people who came for the hook instead of the problem.

16. cta at the end.

17. on a 60s video, under 25% average watch time and tiktok stops pushing it.

kill or keep

18. 10-15 videos per account across every format. comments or 5-10k views = keep going. can't clear 1k views on any account = kill it.

19. every video over 10k views gets 4 questions: which pain point hit, did it reach the right audience, did more product context hurt reach, how do we combine its virality with another video's buying intent.

20. retention tells you what gets views. saves and comments tell you what converts.

21. match view spikes to attribution spikes over the next 72 hours. a video from a month ago can come back and crush.

22. a format is repeatable once it clears 100k views 5 times. after that, expect about 10-15% of videos at similar quality to go viral.

scaling winners

23. repost a winner until it stops working. make 3 iterations on the same concept: hook, wording, visual.

24. put the app name on screen and in the first words of the caption. one of our 7M+ view videos led to 2x that in replies.

25. at 50k views it goes in the bounty channel. creators comment from their personal accounts ("dude same, that's why i use [app]") and we pay out on comments that get likes.

26. then a creator films a reply to the top "wait what app is that?" comment. comment likes are our earliest signal that downloads are coming.

27. every video over 20k views adds the brand as a collaborator on instagram.

28. views but no site visits = fix the ugc. site visits but no conversions = fix onboarding and the product.

most importantly: do not quit at week 3!!
